learn.title: Persistent project guidance
learn.body: A project brief records the shared facts that future tasks should reuse. It keeps goals and decisions visible beyond one request. A tool may load a brief automatically, but a basic API chat does not inherently remember it; make the relevant guidance available.

learn.title: What to include
learn.body: Record the user goal, scope and non-goals. Add a simple architecture map, naming and style conventions, project layout, setup and verification commands, and acceptance checks. Keep entries specific enough to guide a decision or check a result.

learn.title: Keep it current
learn.body: A brief is useful only while it matches the project. Update it when a requirement, command or architectural decision changes. Remove stale instructions and resolve contradictions. A brief should guide work, not preserve every abandoned idea.

learn.title: Draft a habit-tracker brief
learn.body: Turn scattered early decisions into reusable guidance.
steps: Goal: one person records daily habits and reviews recent progress.
Scope: local entries and a summary; non-goals: accounts and social sharing.
Architecture: screens call habit logic; storage owns saved entries.
Conventions and checks: use calendar dates; list the exact setup and test commands.
Acceptance: a saved completion remains after reopening and appears in recent history.

learn.title: Keep guidance actionable
learn.body: Do not turn the brief into a diary or a dump of the entire repository. Link to detailed sources when needed and summarize stable decisions here. For a small task, supply the brief alongside the specific goal and current evidence.
After a meaningful change, ask whether the brief's goal, boundaries, commands or acceptance checks still describe the real project.

questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of a project brief?
choices: Reuse current goals, decisions and checks across tasks
Store every conversation word for word
questions.explanation: A brief provides durable shared guidance. Each task still needs its own goal and evidence, and no document can guarantee a correct answer.

questions.prompt: Update the brief whenever a project decision or command becomes \_\_.
questions.explanation: Outdated guidance can send later work in the wrong direction. Revise or remove entries when the real project changes.

questions.prompt: Match each brief section to a suitable habit-tracker entry.
questions.explanation: Each section answers a different question: why the project exists, what it excludes, how parts connect and what observable result counts as done.

questions.prompt: Put these brief-maintenance actions in order.
steps: Record the current goal, scope and architecture
Add conventions, commands and acceptance checks
Use the brief with a specific task
Revise entries when project decisions change
questions.explanation: Establish the core direction, add working guidance, apply it to real tasks and maintain it as decisions evolve.

questions.prompt: Which change requires a project-brief update?
choices: The project replaces its test command and adds user accounts
A developer fixes a typo in their personal notes
The same requirement is restated in a task
A test is run again without any project change
questions.explanation: New commands and a changed account scope affect future work and verification. The brief should reflect both changes rather than retaining stale guidance.

questions.prompt: What term describes the observable conditions a result must meet to count as done?
questions.explanation: Acceptance criteria, or acceptance checks, describe observable conditions for done. They give builders and reviewers a shared result to verify.
